name: CO2 laser perioral rejuvenation

angle.text: Patients get clinic CO2 laser resurfacing to smooth lines around the mouth and lips. The technique is established for skin rejuvenation, with registered trials on laser resurfacing in general.

summary: Clinic laser resurfacing for lip lines; established technique with registered trials, but downtime and scarring risks apply.
note: Higher hypopigmentation and scarring risk than erbium lasers.
currentQuick:
A clinician uses a CO2 laser to resurface skin around the mouth to soften lines.
Trials are registered, but this article does not summarise results.
How it works: The laser vaporises thin skin layers and heats the dermis, prompting collagen remodelling.
Risks and caveats: Described risks include hypopigmentation, scarring and herpes outbreaks.
deepLead:
CO2 laser perioral rejuvenation uses a carbon dioxide laser to treat lines around the mouth. CO2 lasers emit at 10,600 nm, vaporise tissue and heat the deep dermis, which is thought to stimulate collagen and elastin production.
Several trial registrations cover perioral wrinkles, including a completed fractional CO2 study of 35 participants, but no results are cited here. Sources are limited, so the article is short.

name: Hyaluronidase lip filler dissolving

angle.text: Users and clinicians use it to dissolve hyaluronic acid filler and fix lumpy, uneven or unwanted lip volume. The change is visible as the filler breaks down; evidence for this use is mostly clinical practice.

summary: An enzyme injected to break down hyaluronic acid filler in the lips; the standard reversal route, though evidence here is mostly clinical practice rather than trials.
note: Prescription enzyme; works only on hyaluronic acid fillers, and allergic reactions are possible.
currentQuick:
Hyaluronidase is an enzyme that breaks down hyaluronic acid. Because many lip fillers are made of cross-linked hyaluronic acid, clinicians can inject the enzyme to reduce or remove unwanted filler, such as lumps, migration or an overfilled look.
It is discussed in looksmaxxing spaces as the undo button for lip filler. Wikipedia describes it as the best treatment option for dissolving lip filler or treating related complications.[1]
How it works: The enzyme cleaves the bonds in hyaluronic acid, lowering the viscosity of the gel and letting the body clear the fragments. It does not act on non-hyaluronic fillers such as PMMA or fat.
Risks and caveats: Hyaluronidase is a prescription medicine in the United States, with several animal-derived and recombinant products approved since 2004.[1] Reported concerns include injection-site reactions and, rarely, hypersensitivity. Results depend on the filler type and the practitioner.
deepLead:
Hyaluronidase is a family of enzymes that break down hyaluronic acid, a sugar-based polymer found naturally in connective tissue. Medically it is used to help other drugs and fluids spread through tissue, for example alongside local anesthetics in eye surgery and for fluids given under the skin.
In aesthetic medicine it is injected to dissolve hyaluronic acid-based dermal fillers, including those placed in the lips. Wikipedia describes it as the best treatment option for dissolving lip filler or treating related complications. It does not break down non-hyaluronic fillers, which include several synthetic and permanent materials.
Hyaluronidase products have been FDA-approved in the United States since 2004. Published trial evidence specifically on lip filler dissolving was not located for this article; the clinical literature on the topic consists mainly of clinical practice and case-based reports.

name: Philtrum filler / shortening

chain: Filler or lip lift reshapes upper lip
angle.text: Users have the groove under the nose reshaped with filler or a lip lift so the upper lip looks shorter and more defined. The result is visible once done; formal evidence is limited.

summary: Reshaping the philtrum and cupid's bow with filler or a lip lift to look shorter and more defined; plenty of cosmetic practice, little formal evidence.
note: Surgical versions leave scars; filler carries standard filler risks.
currentQuick:
The philtrum is the groove between the nose and upper lip. Some people seek a shorter philtrum or a sharper cupid's bow, using filler along the lip border or a surgical lip lift.
Surgeons report high satisfaction with lip lifts, but no single technique is standard.[3]
How it works: Filler adds volume at the lip border and philtral columns. A lip lift removes skin below the nose or along the lip border to expose more of the upper lip; a 2014 review found philtrum length decreased with indirect techniques.[3]
Risks and caveats: Lip lift risks include visible scarring, numbness, asymmetry, lip distortion and speech or smile changes.[3] Filler carries bruising, lumps, allergic reactions and, rarely, vascular complications.[2]
deepLead:
The philtrum is the vertical groove in the middle of the upper lip, running from the base of the nose to the lip's upper edge. The cupid's bow is the double curve of the upper lip's border, with peaks lining up with the philtral columns.
Philtrum filler and shortening refer to cosmetic efforts to make this area look shorter, more defined or more lifted, either by injecting filler or by surgical lip lift. Wikipedia's lip lift article describes surgery that makes the vermilion border more prominent and changes the area above the lip.
Published information located for this article is descriptive and surgical; no trial specific to filler shortening of the philtrum was identified.

name: Lip bleaching / lightening laser

angle.text: Users seek lasers or topical agents to lighten darker or pigmented lips for a more even, pinker tone. Evidence specific to lips is scarce.

summary: Procedures, including lasers, aimed at lightening darker or pigmented lips; evidence specific to lips is scarce.
note: Lasers can worsen pigmentation in some skin types.
currentQuick:
Some people with darker or unevenly pigmented lips seek lightening treatments. Clinics offer laser, peels, creams or cosmetic tattooing for this purpose.
Lip color depends on melanin and on blood showing through thin tissue.[2]
How it works: Lasers target melanin. Wikipedia notes that several lasers have been used for melasma with some benefit, but recurrence is common and some can increase pigmentation.[3]
Risks and caveats: Risks reported for pigment-lightening in general include recurrence, post-inflammatory darkening and irritation; people with darker skin are described as more prone to hyperpigmentation.[1][3] No lip-specific trials were found.
deepLead:
Lip bleaching or lightening refers to cosmetic treatments intended to reduce darker pigmentation of the lips, using laser, topical agents or other methods.
Lip skin has only three to five cell layers compared with up to sixteen on typical facial skin. In lighter skin, fewer melanocytes let blood vessels show through, producing a red tone; in darker skin, more melanin makes lips look darker.
General sources describe lasers and intense pulsed light as options for hyperpigmentation, with recurrence common and some lasers capable of increasing pigmentation. No published trial specific to laser lightening of the lips was identified.

name: Lemon and sugar lip lightening

angle.text: DIY posters rub lemon juice and sugar on the lips hoping to lighten them. The lightening is a home-remedy belief that has not been tested for lips.

summary: A DIY scrub of lemon juice and sugar used to lighten lips; untested for this purpose, and lemon juice plus sun can cause skin darkening.
note: Citrus juice on skin followed by sunlight can cause phytophotodermatitis.
currentQuick:
The practice involves rubbing lemon juice, often with sugar as an exfoliant, onto the lips in the hope of lightening them.
No studies of the method for lip color were found.
How it works: Proponents attribute lightening to the acidity of lemon and the abrasion of sugar. Lemon juice is about 5 to 6 percent citric acid.[1]
Risks and caveats: Contact with citrus juice followed by UV exposure can cause phytophotodermatitis, with redness, blistering and lasting brown marks.[2]
deepLead:
Lemon and sugar lip lightening is a home remedy in which lemon juice, usually combined with sugar granules, is applied to or rubbed on the lips with the aim of making them lighter.
Lemon juice contains roughly 5 to 6 percent citric acid. No published study of the mixture for lip pigmentation was identified.
Dermatology sources describe a reaction called phytophotodermatitis, in which light-sensitizing plant compounds such as furanocoumarins on the skin plus UVA exposure cause inflammation and later pigmentation.

name: Honey and beetroot lip remedies

angle.text: Folk-remedy users apply beetroot juice for a natural pink tint and honey for softness. The stain is visible and temporary; no lip studies exist for either.

summary: Folk remedies using honey or beetroot juice for lip color and softness; beetroot stains temporarily, and no lip studies exist.
note: Honey and beet products can cause allergic reactions in some people.
currentQuick:
Honey and beetroot are used in home lip remedies. Honey is applied for moisture, beetroot juice as a natural pink-red tint.
No studies of either for changing lip color were found.
How it works: Beetroot's red pigment is betanin, a betalain used industrially as a red food colorant.[2] Honey has been studied as a wound dressing.[1]
Risks and caveats: Honey can interact with existing allergies according to Wikipedia, and honey is not recommended for infants under one year when eaten.[1]
deepLead:
Honey and beetroot lip remedies are folk practices in which honey is applied to the lips for softness or beetroot juice is applied for a pink or red tint.
Beetroot owes its red color to betanin, which is used commercially as a red food colorant. Honey has antibacterial activity in laboratory settings and preliminary evidence suggests faster healing of partial-thickness burns, but these findings concern wound care, not lip color.
No published study of either substance for lip appearance was identified.

name: Vitamin E / coconut oil lips

angle.text: Users rub vitamin E or coconut oil on the lips at home for softness and to ease chapping. It is plausible as a moisturizer but untested in lip-specific trials.

summary: Home use of vitamin E oil or coconut oil on the lips for softness; plausible as a moisturizer but no lip-specific trials, and vitamin E can cause contact dermatitis.
note: Allergic contact dermatitis has been reported with vitamin E derivatives.
currentQuick:
People apply vitamin E oil or coconut oil to their lips for softness and to counter dryness.
Lips lack sweat glands and dry out and chap more easily than other skin.[3]
How it works: Oils act as occlusive emollients on the surface. Coconut oil is used in cosmetics and soaps, and its fatty acids appear in cosmetic products.[2]
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia notes reviews found insufficient evidence for topical vitamin E claims on wound healing and scarring, and allergic contact dermatitis has been reported with tocopheryl derivatives.[1]
deepLead:
Vitamin E and coconut oil are commonly used in home lip care, applied for softness and to ease chapping.
Lips lack sweat glands, so they dry and chap more easily than other skin. Tocopheryl acetate is widely used in skin-care products, but reviews cited by Wikipedia find insufficient evidence for claims about wound healing and scar reduction.
Allergic contact dermatitis from vitamin E derivatives has been reported. Coconut oil is used industrially in cosmetics and soap. No lip-specific trials of either were identified.

name: Quitting smoking for lips

angle.text: Users quit smoking hoping lips look less dark, thin and lined. Smoker's-face ageing is described in clinical literature, but lip-specific research is lacking.

summary: Stopping tobacco is claimed to improve dark, thin, lined lips; general smoker's-face research exists, lip-specific research does not.
note: Evidence concerns facial ageing in general, not lips specifically.
currentQuick:
Quitting smoking for lips means stopping tobacco in the hope that lips look less dark, thin and lined. It is discussed as a no-cost lifestyle step in skin and lip care.
Smoker's face, a pattern of premature facial ageing, is documented in clinical literature. Studies measuring lip-specific change after quitting were not found.
How it works: Smoking is linked in the literature to higher collagen-degrading enzymes, depleted antioxidants, reduced skin blood flow and oxidative stress. Proponents expect stopping to reduce these effects on the lip and perioral skin.
Risks and caveats: No appearance-related harms of quitting are described in the sources reviewed. Smoking is reported to slow healing after lip procedures such as fillers.
deepLead:
Quitting smoking for lips is a lifestyle practice in which people stop using tobacco in the hope of reducing the dark, thin or lined appearance of the lips and the surrounding skin. It sits within the broader appearance-related idea of "smoker's face", a pattern of premature facial ageing that clinicians have described in people who smoke.
The general link between tobacco smoke and skin ageing is documented in the medical literature, with proposed mechanisms including increased matrix metalloproteinase activity, depleted antioxidants and reduced blood flow to the skin. The sources reviewed for this article do not report studies that measure changes specifically in lip colour, lip thickness or perioral lines after quitting.

name: Lip filler cannula technique

angle.text: Users choose injectors who use a blunt cannula for lip filler, saying it bruises less and is gentler. The filler result is visible; no comparison with needles was found in reviewed sources.

summary: Injecting lip filler with a blunt cannula instead of a needle is touted as gentler; no comparison was found in the sources reviewed.
note: Filler can rarely cause vascular occlusion; technique claims are untested in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
A cannula is a blunt-tipped tube used instead of a sharp needle to place filler in the lips. Proponents say it bruises less and is safer.
The reference sources reviewed describe lip filling with fine needles and do not compare the two methods.
How it works: Filler is deposited through a small entry point along tracks in the lip rather than through multiple needle punctures. The blunt tip is said to move around vessels instead of piercing them.
Risks and caveats: Fillers can cause bruising, swelling, lumps, infection, allergic reaction and rarely blindness or tissue death. Fillers are regulated as medical devices and rules on who may inject vary by country.
deepLead:
Lip filler cannula technique refers to injecting dermal filler into the lips through a blunt-tipped flexible tube (a cannula) rather than a sharp needle. Within appearance communities it is often described as a gentler or safer approach, mainly because proponents say it causes less bruising and lowers the chance of puncturing a blood vessel.
Dermal fillers generally can cause bruising, swelling and, rarely, vascular occlusion with serious consequences. The reference articles reviewed here describe lip filling with fine needles and do not compare cannulas with needles, so the comparative claims below are documented as beliefs rather than as findings from the sources reviewed.

name: Lipstick shade matching

angle.text: Users choose a lipstick colour to suit skin tone and lip shape so the lips look emphasised and the face more harmonious. The colour is visible instantly; effects on attractiveness are untested.

summary: Choosing lipstick colour to suit skin tone and lip shape; history and safety are documented, attractiveness effects are untested.
note: Trace lead and PFAS have been reported in some lipsticks.
currentQuick:
Shade matching means picking a lipstick colour that suits your skin tone and lip shape. It is a removable, low-cost styling approach.
Reference sources cover lipstick history and composition; no studies of shade choice and attractiveness were found.
How it works: Colour and finish change lip contrast and apparent size: matte formulas contain more fillers, glossy ones more oil, and shimmer uses mica or pearl particles.
Risks and caveats: Trace lead has been found in some lipsticks, with the FDA saying levels were not a safety concern and the CDC saying no blood lead level is safe. A 2021 study found fluorine, an indicator of PFAS, in many liquid lipsticks.
deepLead:
Lipstick shade matching is the cosmetic practice of choosing a lip colour to suit a person's skin tone, lip shape and overall look, and in appearance communities it is discussed as a way to emphasise lip shape and facial harmony. Lipstick itself is a wax-based colour product, and lip colour has been worn for thousands of years in many cultures.
The reference sources reviewed describe lipstick history, composition and safety, and do not report controlled studies on how shade choice affects perceived attractiveness. Shade-matching advice is therefore documented here as practitioner and community belief.

name: PLLA / Sculptra perioral

chain: Softer lines, more volume around mouth
angle.text: Patients use poly-L-lactic acid around the mouth to soften wrinkles and restore volume over weeks. Evidence for the perioral area in reviewed sources is one ongoing trial.

summary: A collagen-stimulating injectable used around the mouth; perioral evidence in the sources reviewed is one ongoing trial.
note: Clinician-administered; no perioral trial results available in sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
PLLA is the active ingredient in Sculptra, an injectable that stimulates the skin to make collagen. People use it around the mouth to soften wrinkles and restore support gradually.
A phase 4 trial of topical PLLA with microneedling for perioral wrinkles is recruiting; no results were found.
How it works: The material triggers a foreign-body reaction in which macrophages release signals such as TGF-beta, prompting fibroblasts to produce collagen. It degrades over about six months to two years into lactic acid.
Risks and caveats: Nodules are a recognised concern with injectable collagen stimulators generally, though the sources reviewed did not detail rates. It is a clinician-administered product; rules vary by country.
deepLead:
PLLA / Sculptra perioral refers to the use of poly-L-lactic acid, the active ingredient in the injectable product Sculptra, in the area around the mouth to stimulate collagen and soften wrinkles or restore volume. It is classed as a collagen stimulator rather than an immediate volumising filler.
Poly-L-lactic acid is a biodegradable material. Reference descriptions say it provokes a foreign-body reaction in which macrophages release signalling molecules such as TGF-beta, prompting fibroblasts to produce collagen, and that it has been used in facial volume restoration, notably for HIV-associated lipodystrophy. Evidence specific to the perioral region in the sources reviewed is limited to a registered trial still recruiting.

name: Lip stencil / bone structure hack: orthotropics for lip support

angle.text: Mewing and orthotropics circles claim tongue posture can reshape the bone under the lips to improve profile. Reference sources describe mewing as unproven and do not cover lips.

summary: The claim that mewing reshapes bone to support the lips; reference sources call mewing unproven and do not cover lips.
note: Experts cited say no credible evidence supports mewing changing facial structure.
currentQuick:
This is the idea that mewing, a tongue and jaw posture practice from orthotropics, can change the lip profile by altering the bone beneath the lips.
Reference sources describe mewing as unproven and say orthodontic bodies see no evidence it reshapes the jaw.
How it works: Practitioners press the tongue against the palate and keep a sealed-lip, nasal-breathing posture, believing sustained posture shifts jaw growth and facial support.
Risks and caveats: Potential risks cited include jaw joint problems, bite changes and delayed orthodontic care in children.
deepLead:
This entry covers the claim, circulated in mewing and orthotropics circles, that jaw and facial posture training can change the profile of the lips by altering the bone structure that supports them. Mewing is a form of oral posture training associated with orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike Mew, built on tongue pressure against the palate.
The reference sources reviewed describe mewing as unproven, state that the American Association of Orthodontists sees no evidence that it improves the jaw, and do not address lips or soft-tissue profile specifically.

name: Lip competence training

angle.text: Oral-posture communities practice resting with sealed lips, claiming it supports jaw and facial development. Lip competence is a real orthodontic descriptor, but training it for this outcome is untested.

summary: Keeping the lips sealed at rest as a posture habit; claimed to aid facial growth, untested as training.
note: Mouth taping, sometimes used for lip closure, is described as carrying risks.
currentQuick:
Lip competence training means keeping the lips lightly sealed at rest. Some oral-posture communities treat it as part of mewing.
In clinical writing, lip competence is a descriptor of whether lips close at rest. No study tests training it for facial change.
How it works: Practitioners close the lips softly and breathe through the nose, as part of a routine with tongue posture.
Risks and caveats: Reference sources say mouth taping used to encourage lip closure carries risks and needs professional supervision.
deepLead:
Lip competence training is the habit of keeping the lips gently sealed at rest, treated in some oral-posture communities as a posture skill that is said to support jaw and facial development. In orthodontics, lip competence is a clinical descriptor meaning the lips can close at rest without strain, and lip incompetence means they cannot.
A sealed-lip position is also listed as a core element of mewing, alongside tongue posture, lightly touching teeth and nasal breathing. No reviewed study tests whether training lip closure changes facial structure.

name: Cryolipolysis (CoolSculpting Mini Chin)

angle.text: Users seek fat-freezing under the chin for a sharper jawline without surgery. It is FDA-cleared for the area, with modest measured fat reduction in studies.

summary: Fat freezing under the chin: a cleared non-surgical option with modest measured fat reduction and a rare paradoxical-growth side effect.
note: Reviews rate data quality as low; rare paradoxical adipose hyperplasia (enlargement of treated fat) has been reported.
currentQuick:
Cryolipolysis is a non-invasive procedure that uses controlled cold to reduce small pockets of fat. Under the chin (the submental area, often called a double chin) it is one of the treatment sites cleared by the US FDA, and a smaller applicator is sometimes marketed as a mini-chin treatment.
In looksmaxxing discussions it is raised as a non-surgical way to sharpen the jaw-neck line. Systematic reviews report modest average reductions in fat thickness, and the evidence base is described by reviewers as low in quality.
How it works: A device cools the skin and underlying subcutaneous fat over a set period. Cold is intended to damage fat tissue in the treated area, which the body then gradually clears. Reviews measure the result as skinfold or ultrasound fat-thickness change over following months.
Risks and caveats: Commonly reported effects are redness, numbness, swelling, bruising and mild pain, usually resolving within weeks. A rare effect, paradoxical adipose hyperplasia, in which the treated fat enlarges, is reported at roughly 0.12% to 1.0% depending on the study, and surgical options such as liposuction are described for treating it.
deepLead:
Cryolipolysis, commonly called fat freezing and sold under the CoolSculpting brand, is a non-invasive procedure that uses extreme cold applied to the skin to reduce subcutaneous fat in targeted areas . The submental area under the chin is one of the sites for which the US FDA has cleared the technique, alongside the jawline, arms, flanks, abdomen and thighs .
In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a non-surgical route to a more defined jaw-neck angle, sometimes under the label mini chin, referring to a smaller applicator used for the chin area. Systematic reviews of cryolipolysis in general report average fat-thickness reductions of a few millimeters and high patient satisfaction, while rating the quality of the data as low .

name: Lipodissolve / PC-DC injections

angle.text: Users have had PC/DC injections to shrink small fat pockets, including under the chin. The FDA has warned about these mixtures; the only approved injectable is a separate deoxycholic acid product.

summary: Injected fat-dissolving mixtures (phosphatidylcholine/deoxycholate) that have drawn FDA warnings; the only approved injectable is a separate deoxycholic acid product.
note: FDA sent warning letters in 2010 on unapproved lipodissolve products; case reports include infection, scarring and nodules.
currentQuick:
Lipodissolve, also called injection lipolysis or PC/DC injections, is the practice of injecting a mixture, usually phosphatidylcholine and sodium deoxycholate, into subcutaneous fat to reduce small deposits. In looksmaxxing circles it is mentioned for double chin and facial fat.
Published support consists mostly of retrospective series and practitioner reports; a review noted that no placebo-controlled studies have shown safety or efficacy. A separate, FDA-approved deoxycholic acid product (Kybella) exists for submental fullness.
How it works: The detergent-like components are described as disrupting fat cell membranes, causing local fat cell breakdown and an inflammatory response that is followed by tissue remodeling. Practitioners also claim skin tightening.
Risks and caveats: The FDA stated that lipodissolve products are not approved for fat removal and received reports of scarring, skin deformation and painful lumps. Case reports describe infections, including a nontuberculous mycobacterial infection. Professional societies in plastic surgery and dermatologic surgery have issued warnings.
deepLead:
Lipodissolve, also called injection lipolysis or PC/DC injections, refers to injecting drug mixtures into subcutaneous fat to destroy fat cells. Most formulations are based on phosphatidylcholine (PC) and sodium deoxycholate (DC) . Practitioners have used it for small localized deposits, including under the chin.
Authors of practitioner-written papers report reductions in localized fat and some skin retraction, and describe the method as an alternative or adjunct to liposuction . A review noted that no placebo-controlled studies have established safety or efficacy, though many retrospective reports describe benefit . In 2010 the US FDA sent warning letters over lipodissolve marketing .

name: Laser lipolysis (SmartLipo)

angle.text: Users consider laser-assisted fat removal for the neck and jawline for a leaner contour and some skin tightening. Early studies report fat reduction and tightening.

summary: Laser-assisted fat removal that heats fat through a small cannula, with early studies reporting fat reduction and some skin tightening.
note: A minimally invasive surgical procedure; published work is mostly small series and tissue studies.
currentQuick:
Laser lipolysis, best known by the SmartLipo brand, is a minimally invasive procedure in which a laser fiber is passed through a small incision to liquefy or heat fat, often followed by suction. It is discussed in looksmaxxing spaces for the jawline and neck.
The early literature, much of it practitioner-written, reports fat reduction and skin tightening. Most published studies are small, histology or modeling studies, or retrospective series.
How it works: Laser energy at wavelengths such as 1064, 1320 or 1444 nm is absorbed by fat tissue, disrupting fat cells and heating the surrounding tissue. Authors claim the heating also stimulates collagen and skin contraction.
Risks and caveats: It is a surgical procedure with risks shared with liposuction, such as bleeding, infection, numbness and contour irregularities. Heating of tissue is a specific consideration, and thermal studies have examined temperature rise in treated tissue.
deepLead:
Laser lipolysis, also called laser-assisted liposuction or by the SmartLipo brand, uses laser energy delivered through a thin fiber under the skin to disrupt fat cells, sometimes followed by suction removal. It is promoted for small areas, including the neck and jawline, and for tightening skin .
Early reports described a less traumatic technique than conventional liposuction with reduced bleeding and skin retraction . Subsequent work includes a 30-subject Nd:YAG study , histologic and thermal studies , and a retrospective analysis of 534 procedures with a diode laser . General liposuction carries recognized risks, which a Wikipedia overview summarizes .

name: Body recomposition / calorie deficit

angle.text: Users cut calories, often with protein and lifting, to lose body fat and reveal facial structure. Fat loss cannot be targeted to the face, and the approach is widely studied for general fat loss.

summary: Eating below maintenance to lose body fat, including from the face, usually paired with protein and lifting; fat loss cannot be targeted to the face.
note: Aggressive deficits carry documented risks; looksmaxxing forum users debate deficits during puberty.
currentQuick:
A calorie deficit means eating less energy than the body uses, so stored fat is drawn on. In looksmaxxing it is the common answer to facial fat: people say lowering overall body fat reveals the jaw and cheekbones. Body recomposition refers to losing fat while keeping or building muscle.
Reference sources describe energy balance as the basis of fat loss. Forum discussion focuses on how large a deficit to run, body-fat targets, and whether cutting during puberty affects growth.
How it works: When intake is below expenditure, hormonal changes favor releasing fatty acids from fat stores. Reference material recommends adequate protein and resistance training to help retain lean mass during a deficit, and notes the body adapts, so weight loss often falls short of simple arithmetic.
Risks and caveats: Reference sources list fatigue, irritability, hair loss and menstrual irregularities in the short term, and nutrient deficiency, muscle loss, bone density loss and gallstones with very large deficits. Adolescents are named as a group vulnerable to progression from restrictive dieting to an eating disorder.
deepLead:
A calorie deficit occurs when energy intake is lower than total daily energy expenditure, so the body supplies the shortfall mainly from stored fat . Body recomposition is the related goal of reducing fat while maintaining or increasing lean mass, typically discussed alongside resistance training and higher protein intake .
In looksmaxxing communities it is the standard approach to facial fat: proponents say that reducing overall body fat is how the jawline and cheekbones become more visible, and forum threads debate target body-fat percentages, deficit size and timing . A reference summary describes a sustainable deficit and warns that large deficits carry risks .

name: Low-sodium / low-carb face de-bloat

angle.text: Users cut salt and carbs before photos or events to drop facial water retention. The sodium-fluid link is documented, but no study tests this for facial appearance.

summary: Cutting salt and carbs to shed facial water retention; the general link between sodium and fluid is documented, but no study tests it for facial appearance.
note: Persistent or sudden facial swelling can reflect medical causes.
currentQuick:
This practice involves reducing dietary sodium and carbohydrates to reduce water held in the face and body, with the aim of a leaner-looking jaw and cheeks.
Medical references describe sodium retention as one mechanism of edema, but the sources reviewed here include no studies of low-sodium or low-carb diets for facial appearance.
How it works: Medical references describe fluid shifting between blood vessels and tissue according to pressures, with kidney sodium and water retention one driver of raised pressure. When sodium retention is the mechanism, lowering salt intake is one described management.
Risks and caveats: Medical references note that facial and eye-area swelling, particularly sudden or painful swelling, can reflect underlying conditions and call for clinical attention.
deepLead:
Low-sodium and low-carb face de-bloating refers to adjusting diet, mainly salt and carbohydrate intake, to reduce fluid retention that practitioners say blurs facial definition. It is typically a short-term practice used before photos or events.
Medical references describe edema as fluid buildup in tissue and list sodium retention among its mechanisms, with reduced salt intake used in management when sodium retention is the cause . Swelling around the eyes is usually most noticeable right after waking, and facial swelling from lying flat typically resolves after time upright . No studies found test dietary sodium or carbohydrate changes on facial appearance.

name: Face slimming massage / lymphatic drainage

chain: Massage or gua sha moves fluid
angle.text: Forum users massage the face or use gua sha to shift fluid and look less puffy and more defined. Proponents describe fluid redistribution, not fat loss; no studies on facial slimming were found.

summary: Facial massage and gua sha to move fluid and reduce puffiness; popular in forums, with no studies on facial slimming found.
note: Evidence for manual lymphatic drainage is in lymphedema, not facial appearance.
currentQuick:
Face slimming massage covers light massage, often modeled on manual lymphatic drainage, and tools like gua sha, used to reduce facial puffiness. Forum guides describe doing it several times a day, sometimes with jump rope and icing.
Manual lymphatic drainage has been studied mainly in lymphedema, where a 2013 meta-analysis found no clear evidence it prevents or treats arm swelling after breast cancer. No studies found test it for facial slimming.
How it works: Proponents say gentle strokes move excess interstitial fluid along lymphatic pathways, reducing puffiness rather than fat. Manual lymphatic drainage is described in reference sources as a light-pressure technique intended to encourage lymph flow toward the heart.
Risks and caveats: Gua sha nearly always causes minor skin trauma such as redness and bruising, and rarely more serious injuries are reported. Reference sources do not address the safety of facial manual lymphatic drainage.
deepLead:
Face slimming massage refers to facial massage techniques, often adapted from manual lymphatic drainage (MLD), and tools such as gua sha used to reduce facial puffiness and improve definition. Proponents say the effect is fluid redistribution, not fat loss .
MLD is a light-pressure technique developed by Danish practitioners Emil and Estrid Vodder in the 1930s, and its main medical application is lymphedema . A 2013 systematic review of randomized trials in breast cancer-related lymphedema found no clear evidence that MLD prevents or treats limb swelling . No studies found test facial massage for slimming.

name: Chewing gum for face fat

angle.text: Appearance forum users chew gum hoping to burn cheek fat and slim the face. This rests on spot reduction, which exercise research does not support, and no trial tests it.

summary: The idea that chewing gum melts cheek fat; it rests on spot reduction, which exercise research does not support, and no trial tests it.
note: No study has tested gum for facial fat; spot reduction is not supported by exercise research.
currentQuick:
Some looksmaxxing circles say that chewing gum for long stretches slims the cheeks and sharpens the jawline by burning facial fat.
The idea is a version of spot reduction. Exercise research cited in encyclopedic sources reports that working a muscle does not selectively reduce the fat above it, and no trial has examined gum and facial fat.
How it works: Proponents say repeated chewing works the jaw and cheek muscles and burns local fat. Physiologists cited in the literature say fat is lost from the whole body through overall energy balance, with distribution largely set by genetics.
Risks and caveats: Gum is generally regarded as low risk. Sorbitol-sweetened gum in large amounts may cause gas or diarrhea. No studies found on facial-fat effects.
deepLead:
Chewing gum for face fat is the belief, found in appearance-focused online communities, that repeatedly chewing gum burns fat in the cheeks and jaw area or slims the face. It belongs to the wider family of facial-slimming ideas that assume working a local muscle will reduce the fat over it.
Spot reduction, the general principle behind this idea, is described in encyclopedic sources as the claim that exercising one muscle group reduces fat in the area around it. Reviews of exercise studies cited there report that fat is lost from the whole body through diet and overall energy balance rather than from the exercised site. No published human trial found in the sources reviewed for this article has tested chewing gum specifically for facial fat.
Chewing gum has been studied for other outcomes, including short-term memory, dental plaque and recovery of bowel function after abdominal surgery.
